q: Neurons, skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and red blood cells are classic examples of which category of cell based on regenerative capacity?

e.correcta: Permanent cells are terminally differentiated and have exited the cell cycle (remaining in G0), so they cannot regenerate after injury; lost tissue is instead replaced by fibrosis or scar. Neurons and cardiac/skeletal myocytes lack the machinery to re-enter mitosis, and mature RBCs are anucleate and cannot divide at all, which is why myocardial infarction and neuronal injury heal with scar tissue rather than functional tissue regrowth.

incorrectas.A: Labile cells (e.g., epidermis, GI epithelium, bone marrow hematopoietic cells) continuously cycle and regenerate rapidly throughout life, the opposite of the non-dividing tissues listed here.
incorrectas.B: Stable (quiescent) cells, like hepatocytes and proximal tubule cells, normally sit in G0 but retain the capacity to re-enter the cell cycle and proliferate when needed (e.g., liver regeneration); neurons and cardiac myocytes lack this reserve capacity.
incorrectas.D: Pluripotent stem cells can differentiate into any cell type and self-renew indefinitely; mature neurons, myocytes, and RBCs are fully differentiated end cells, not stem cells.

q: Hepatocytes, lymphocytes, proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) cells, and periosteal cells are classic examples of which category of cell based on regenerative capacity?

e.correcta: Stable (quiescent) cells normally reside in the G0 phase of the cell cycle but retain the ability to re-enter G1 and proliferate in response to injury or loss of tissue mass. Hepatocytes exemplify this well, as the liver can regenerate substantially after partial resection, and PCT cells can proliferate to repair the tubule after acute tubular necrosis. This intermediate regenerative capacity distinguishes them from constantly dividing labile cells and from non-dividing permanent cells.

incorrectas.A: Permanent cells (neurons, cardiac and skeletal muscle) are terminally differentiated and cannot re-enter the cell cycle at all, whereas hepatocytes and PCT cells clearly can proliferate when stimulated.
incorrectas.B: Labile cells divide continuously and rapidly throughout life (e.g., bone marrow, gut epithelium, epidermis) to maintain normal turnover, unlike hepatocytes and PCT cells which are normally quiescent and only proliferate on demand.
incorrectas.D: "Terminally differentiated" describes permanent cells that have permanently lost proliferative capacity, which is the opposite of stable cells that can still divide when needed.

q: On the ventral view of the brainstem shown in the image, the boxed 'ID' label marks a nerve rootlet emerging at the cerebellopontine angle, just lateral to the abducens nerve and near the facial nerve exit point. Which cranial nerve is this?

e.correcta: CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) emerges from the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction, at the cerebellopontine angle, immediately adjacent to CN VII. It carries special sensory fibers for hearing (cochlear division) and balance (vestibular division), and this exit point is clinically important because tumors here (vestibular schwannomas) classically compress both CN VII and CN VIII together.

incorrectas.A: CN VII (facial) exits right next to CN VIII at the same cerebellopontine angle, but it is the nerve running slightly more medially/anteriorly toward the internal acoustic meatus, carrying motor fibers to facial expression muscles — it is not the rootlet marked here, which corresponds to the more posterolateral vestibulocochlear root.
incorrectas.C: CN IX (glossopharyngeal) exits from the medulla more caudally, below the pontomedullary junction, as part of a series of rootlets alongside CN X and XI along the postolivary sulcus — its exit point is distinctly lower than the ID marker shown.
incorrectas.D: CN V (trigeminal) exits from the mid-pons, well rostral to the pontomedullary junction, as a large single root — its location is clearly more superior than the structure marked in this image.

q: In the ventral brainstem image, the boxed 'ID' label points to a smooth oval elevation on the anterolateral surface of the medulla, lateral to the pyramid. Which structure produces this surface bulge?

e.correcta: The olive is the oval prominence on the ventrolateral medulla, produced by the underlying inferior olivary nucleus, which sits just lateral to the pyramid and posterior to the exit of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) rootlets. The inferior olivary nucleus relays proprioceptive and motor-error signals to the contralateral cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle, playing a key role in motor learning and coordination.

incorrectas.A: The cerebral peduncle is a midbrain structure carrying descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers on the ventral midbrain surface — it is located far rostral to the medulla and does not correspond to this lateral medullary bulge.
incorrectas.B: The facial colliculus is a small elevation on the dorsal (not ventral) surface of the pons, caused by the abducens nucleus and the looping facial nerve fibers around it — it is not visible on this ventral view and is unrelated to the olive.
incorrectas.D: The gracile tubercle is a small dorsal medullary elevation overlying the nucleus gracilis, part of the dorsal column pathway — it is a posterior structure, not the ventrolateral bulge highlighted here.

q: On the ventral brainstem image, the boxed 'ID' label marks a series of rootlets arising in a line along the postolivary sulcus, just caudal to the vagus nerve (CN X) rootlets and rostral to the cervical spinal roots. Which cranial nerve is this?

e.correcta: The accessory nerve (CN XI) has a unique dual origin: cranial rootlets from the caudal medulla and, more prominently, spinal rootlets that arise from the upper cervical spinal cord (C1-C5) and ascend through the foramen magnum before exiting the skull via the jugular foramen. This is why its rootlets are seen emerging in a line extending down past the medulla into the cervical cord region, distinguishing it from the purely medullary cranial nerves above it.

incorrectas.A: CN XII (hypoglossal) exits from the ventral medulla via the preolivary sulcus, medial to the olive and between the olive and pyramid, not from the postolivary sulcus where CN IX, X, and XI arise — its position is clearly more medial/anterior than the structure marked here.
incorrectas.B: CN X (vagus) does exit from the postolivary sulcus but rostral to CN XI's rootlets, immediately below CN IX — the marked rootlets in this image are caudal to that position, extending down toward the spinal cord, which is characteristic of CN XI rather than CN X.
incorrectas.C: CN IX (glossopharyngeal) is the most rostral of the postolivary sulcus rootlets, exiting just below the pontomedullary junction — it is positioned well above the rootlets marked here, which extend down into the upper cervical region.

q: On the cross-section of the rostral medulla shown, the labeled structure sits at the lateral edge of the tegmentum, just deep to the inferior cerebellar peduncle and adjacent to the incoming fibers of cranial nerve VIII. Which nucleus occupies this position?

e.correcta: The spinal trigeminal nucleus runs as a long column along the lateral medulla, extending from the pons down into the upper cervical spinal cord, and receives pain and temperature fibers from the face via the spinal trigeminal tract that courses just superficial to it. At the level of the rostral medulla it sits lateral and slightly ventral to the inferior cerebellar peduncle, near where CN VIII, IX, and X fibers emerge, which matches the labeled position in the image. Damage here (as in lateral medullary/Wallenberg syndrome) causes loss of pain and temperature on the ipsilateral face.

incorrectas.A: The cochlear nuclei (dorsal and ventral) sit even more laterally, right at the junction where CN VIII enters the brainstem, external to the inferior cerebellar peduncle rather than deep to it, and they process auditory rather than facial sensory information.
incorrectas.C: The nucleus ambiguus lies deeper and more medially in the medullary reticular formation, ventral to the labeled position, and gives rise to motor fibers for CN IX, X, and XI to the pharynx and larynx rather than sensory input from the face.
incorrectas.D: The inferior olivary complex forms the large, wavy-bordered oval in the ventral medulla, a very distinct and much more medial/ventral landmark than the lateral position marked here, and it functions in motor coordination via projections to the cerebellum, not somatosensory relay.

q: On this cross-sectional diagram of the eye, the labeled structure is the site in the posterior pole where retinal ganglion cell axons converge and exit the globe alongside the central retinal artery and vein. Which structure is labeled?

e.correcta: The optic disc is the point on the posterior retina where axons from retinal ganglion cells bundle together to form the optic nerve and exit the eye, and it is also where the central retinal artery and vein enter/exit the globe — exactly the region highlighted in the diagram just anterior to the optic nerve. Because it contains no photoreceptors, it corresponds to the physiologic blind spot on visual field testing, and it can appear swollen (papilledema) with raised intracranial pressure.

incorrectas.B: The fovea is a small pit within the macula, temporal to the optic disc, packed densely with cones and responsible for the sharpest visual acuity — it is a distinct retinal landmark, not the location where the nerve and vessels exit.
incorrectas.A: The ora serrata is the scalloped junction between the retina and the ciliary body found at the periphery of the retina anteriorly, far from the posterior pole region labeled in this image.
incorrectas.C: The macula is the broader region of the central retina surrounding the fovea, responsible for central and color vision, but it is a retinal area for photoreceptor-based vision, not the exit point for the optic nerve and central retinal vessels.

q: On this inferior view of the brain showing its arterial supply, the labeled vessel ('ID') runs along the upper border of the pons toward the cerebellum, just below the level of the posterior cerebral artery and above the paramedian pontine perforators. Which artery is indicated?

e.correcta: The superior cerebellar artery arises from the distal basilar artery just before it bifurcates into the two posterior cerebral arteries, and it courses around the upper pons/midbrain junction to supply the superior surface of the cerebellum, the cerebellar nuclei, and part of the middle cerebellar peduncle. Its position on this diagram — just below the posterior cerebral artery and above the mid-pontine perforating branches — matches this superior, rostral location along the brainstem. Occlusion produces ipsilateral limb/gait ataxia along with contralateral pain/temperature loss due to involvement of the spinothalamic tract.

incorrectas.A: PICA arises from the vertebral artery at the medulla, the most caudal of the three cerebellar arteries — it would be labeled much lower on this diagram, near the medulla, not at the upper pons/midbrain junction.
incorrectas.B: AICA arises from the proximal basilar artery at the level of the mid-to-lower pons, positioned between PICA (lowest) and SCA (highest); its expected label would sit below the level shown for this vessel, not level with the pons-midbrain junction near the PCA origin.
incorrectas.D: The anterior spinal artery runs along the ventral midline of the spinal cord and medulla, formed by branches of the vertebral arteries — it would appear at the very bottom of a brainstem diagram, not laterally near the upper pons.

q: On this lateral diagram of the cerebral cortex, the labeled region ('ID') lies in the frontal lobe, anterior to the premotor cortex and central sulcus. Damage here classically produces a gaze deviation toward the side of the lesion. Which cortical area is indicated?

e.correcta: The frontal eye field, Brodmann area 8, sits in the posterior middle frontal gyrus, anterior to the premotor cortex and rostral to the primary motor strip at the central sulcus — exactly the position marked in this diagram. It controls voluntary saccadic eye movements toward the contralateral visual field; a destructive lesion causes the eyes to deviate toward the side of the lesion (away from the hemiparetic side), while an irritative lesion (e.g., seizure focus) drives the eyes away from the lesion.

incorrectas.A: Primary motor cortex (area 4) sits directly at the precentral gyrus bordering the central sulcus, posterior to both the frontal eye field and premotor cortex, and controls contralateral voluntary movement rather than conjugate gaze.
incorrectas.C: Wernicke's area (area 22) is located in the posterior superior temporal gyrus near the temporo-parietal junction, far posterior to the frontal lobe location shown, and is involved in language comprehension, not eye movements.
incorrectas.D: Prefrontal association cortex occupies the anterior-most frontal lobe and mediates executive function and personality, sitting further rostral than the marked structure, which is positioned closer to the motor strip.

q: On this same lateral cortical diagram, the label ('ID') now marks a band immediately anterior to the central sulcus (Rolando) and posterior to the frontal eye field. Lesions here impair the planning and coordination of complex, learned voluntary movements. Which region is this?

e.correcta: The premotor cortex, Brodmann area 6, forms a vertical band immediately anterior to the primary motor cortex at the central sulcus, matching the position marked here between the central sulcus and the more rostral frontal eye field. It is involved in planning and preparing movements, integrating sensory information to guide motor output, and helping select and sequence learned motor programs before area 4 executes them; lesions here can produce apraxia-like planning deficits without frank paralysis.

incorrectas.B: Primary somatosensory cortex lies on the postcentral gyrus, posterior to the central sulcus, and processes touch, proprioception, and vibration — the diagram marks a location anterior to the central sulcus, in the frontal (motor), not parietal (sensory), lobe.
incorrectas.C: The supplementary motor area is part of area 6 but occupies the medial and superior frontal surface near the interhemispheric fissure, not the lateral convexity band shown in this image, and area 6 as labeled here refers to the broader lateral premotor region.
incorrectas.D: The angular gyrus (area 39) is a parietal-lobe structure near the parieto-temporo-occipital junction, involved in language and reading, and sits far posterior to the frontal premotor strip depicted in the image.

q: Which formula, shown in the image, is used to estimate the volume of distribution (Vd) of a drug?

o.B: Vd = (bioavailability x dose) / plasma concentration at time zero

e.correcta: The image depicts the standard equation Vd = amount of drug in the body / plasma drug concentration, which in practice is estimated as Vd = (F x dose) / Cp0, where F is bioavailability and Cp0 is the extrapolated plasma concentration at time zero. This formula conceptually asks how large a volume the drug would need to occupy, at the concentration measured in plasma, to account for the entire dose administered — a low Vd implies the drug stays mostly in the vasculature, while a high Vd implies extensive tissue distribution.

incorrectas.A: Clearance / elimination rate constant (CL/ke) is actually an alternative, mathematically equivalent way to calculate Vd, but it is not the formula shown in this image, which specifically depicts the dose-and-concentration-based definition.
incorrectas.C: Half-life is related to Vd and clearance by t1/2 = 0.693 x Vd / CL, but this expression calculates half-life, not volume of distribution itself, and does not match the equation pictured.
incorrectas.D: Maintenance dose / clearance describes how to calculate a steady-state plasma concentration or dosing rate, not the volume of distribution.

q: A thin blood smear from a febrile returning traveler shows the form pictured: a red blood cell almost entirely filled by a large, irregularly shaped, dark purple-staining parasite with multiple discrete chromatin dots. Which stage of the Plasmodium life cycle is shown?

e.correcta: The schizont is the intraerythrocytic stage in which the parasite has undergone multiple rounds of nuclear division, producing many individual merozoites clustered together within the red cell — visible on smear as a large, densely packed mass with several separate chromatin dots, as seen in the image. When the schizont matures, the infected red cell ruptures and releases the merozoites into the bloodstream to invade new erythrocytes, which is the event that produces the cyclic fevers of malaria.

incorrectas.A: A ring form is an early, small trophozoite with a thin rim of cytoplasm and a single chromatin dot, giving a signet-ring appearance — far smaller and less complex than the multi-nucleated mass shown here.
incorrectas.B: Gametocytes are the sexual stage taken up by the mosquito vector; Plasmodium falciparum gametocytes have a distinctive crescent or banana shape, quite different from the round, multi-nucleated schizont pictured.
incorrectas.D: Sporozoites are the infective form injected by the mosquito into the human host; they circulate briefly and invade hepatocytes, and are not a stage seen packed inside a red blood cell on a blood smear.

q: The image lists a group of anti-HIV drugs (abacavir, didanosine, emtricitabine, lamivudine, stavudine, tenofovir, zidovudine) that share a common suffix pattern such as "-vudine." These drugs, which require intracellular phosphorylation to compete with natural nucleotides for incorporation into viral DNA, belong to which drug class?

e.correcta: The drugs listed in the image (abacavir, didanosine, emtricitabine, lamivudine, stavudine, tenofovir, zidovudine) are all nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs). They are synthetic analogs of natural nucleosides that must be phosphorylated intracellularly to their active triphosphate forms, after which they compete with endogenous nucleotides for incorporation by HIV reverse transcriptase and act as chain terminators because they lack a 3'-OH group needed for the next phosphodiester bond.

incorrectas.B: Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (e.g., raltegravir, dolutegravir) block the integrase enzyme from inserting proviral DNA into the host genome, a completely different step and mechanism from the reverse transcriptase inhibition shown here.
incorrectas.A: NNRTIs (e.g., efavirenz, nevirapine) also inhibit reverse transcriptase but do so by binding an allosteric site on the enzyme rather than acting as nucleoside analogs requiring phosphorylation, and they do not share the "-vudine"-type naming pattern seen in this list.
incorrectas.C: Protease inhibitors (e.g., ritonavir, indinavir, saquinavir) block the HIV protease enzyme needed to cleave polyprotein precursors into mature viral proteins, acting at a later stage of the viral life cycle than reverse transcription.

q: A 58-year-old man with essential hypertension is newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Which class of antihypertensive should become first-line therapy in this patient because of its renoprotective effect, independent of blood pressure lowering?

e.correcta: ACE inhibitors and ARBs preferentially dilate the efferent glomerular arteriole by blocking angiotensin II, which reduces intraglomerular pressure and hyperfiltration — the mechanism that drives progression of diabetic nephropathy. This renoprotective benefit is independent of their blood-pressure-lowering effect, which is why they become first-line in hypertensive patients with diabetes (or any patient with proteinuric kidney disease), alongside calcium channel blockers, thiazides, and beta-blockers as reasonable add-ons.

incorrectas.A: Loop diuretics are reserved for volume overload states (e.g., heart failure, edema) or when renal function is significantly impaired; they are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension and offer no specific protection against diabetic glomerular injury.
incorrectas.C: Alpha-1 blockers are typically used for hypertension with comorbid benign prostatic hyperplasia, not diabetes, and lack the efferent arteriolar vasodilation that confers renoprotection in diabetic nephropathy.
incorrectas.D: Central alpha-2 agonists (e.g., clonidine) are generally reserved for resistant hypertension or specific situations like pregnancy-associated hypertension; they have no proven specific protective role in diabetic kidney disease.
